title: The Formation of the Body and the Soul
english: He demonstrates, through 'your hands have made me' the creative aspect, and through 'after these things, having changed me, you have struck me' the providential aspect. For this is the work of God's providence: to surround the brave man with distress through struggle, so that he may set up a character and a goal for men, whom they become imitators of when looking toward him. But 'having changed' should be understood as 'having made a change concerning me' regarding the body; for he has struck and wounded him, being utterly desolate of all those who have been changed around him. 'Remember that you formed me of clay, and to dust you turn me back again' (Job 10:9).

Consequently, knowing Him as the Author and Lord of both creation and providence, the word turns to Him in prayer, saying: even if you have brought things upon me as if exercising authority over painful things, yet remember that I am weak and have a constitution from clay—this, however, should be understood concerning the body—and having formed me, you turn me back to dust again. And it is clear from this that he speaks concerning the body; for the soul is not turned back to dust. The things concerning the weakness of human nature proceed to exhort even friends to endurance and the knowledge of His virtue and His patience.

And now, as it is possible to fashion the body, he joined it; for fashioning is possible in type; for it is not said concerning the angels: 'He who fashioned angels,' but 'He who makes His messengers spirits.' And concerning the earth, it is said as a thick body: 'and His hands fashioned the dry land.' These things are not said to mean that God kneads with hands according to human ways, but that to each, divine discipline brings a name that is appropriate: the fashioning, as we have said, to the body, and the making to the soul. Similar to 'and to dust you turn me back again' is that which was said to Adam: 'Dust you are and to dust you shall return' (Gen 3:19).

Observe that if something is said concerning a composite, it is not necessary to understand it concerning every part. For if it is said: 'And David was meek' or 'Moses,' we do not understand this concerning his body. But if: 'And David was red with beauty of eyes,' we think this concerning his body, not concerning the soul. And here, where it is said: 'and to dust you turn me back again,' it is not necessary to calculate that this is said concerning the soul. 'Did you not curdle me like milk, and harden me like cheese?' (Job 10:10). The seed, from which [he] consists...

Regarding the living being, he says, 'as milk unmilked'; and just as milk, being curdled, becomes cheese, so also the seed, being congealed, becomes a nature. And this is the constitution before the embryo. For the seed cast into the channels of the womb, when it is curdled like cheese, becomes a nature; which moreover is spread out or, as the Scripture says, 'is imprinted' (Job 10:9) and receives [it] like a character. But when the limbs differentiate and each becomes its own and moves, for instance, like an animal's hand or foot, then the birth of the embryo clearly demonstrates the living being.

All these things, therefore, encompass, signifying through 'Remember that you formed me of clay' (Job 10:8) the creation of Adam from the beginning, and through 'You did not milk me as milk' (Job 10:10) the successive generations composed by succession. All these things, therefore, he will carry through, indicating the handiwork of God, so that through this or through prayer, one may be called to mercy.

The 'You milked' therefore, he says, showing to God, that by His energy the genuine deposition of the seeds occurs. 'Having clothed me in skin and flesh, and having placed me in bones and nerves.' This is used by those desiring to show that those whom God clothed in skin tunics, these thick things, are their bodies. For it is also said in Genesis: 'And God made skin tunics for Adam and his wife and clothed them' (Gen 3:21). But 'He made for Adam and his wife,' in order to show that He has made a garment suitable for 'male and female.'

It is clear that 'skin and flesh' here signifies the body; for he connects what follows by saying: 'and placed me in bones and nerves.' Thus he announces the whole way and the harmony of the body's constitution through those things before these and through those contained within. It should be noted that these words appear to belong to the soul; for this is the one having clothed herself, having entered into skin and flesh and bones and nerves; which signifies that she precedes the garments and the being clothed; for the subject is 'clothed.' 'And you have provided life and mercy for me, and your oversight has preserved my spirit' (Job 10:12). Since the skin and the flesh and the bones and nerves themselves do not have life by themselves, but have vital movements by the presence of the soul—for when it withdraws, it has nothing vital—he says that you did not only form and...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Possibility of God and the Nature of Sin
english: Having made me consisting of flesh and skin and bone and nerves, you clothed me, but also, 'you have practiced life and mercy toward me.' Through 'life' it signifies that the creation is placed in existence, but through 'mercy' the providential grace. For since it happens that one must also endure attacks against such a life, there is a need for mercy, as it is said: 'you have practiced life and mercy toward me.' For the Creator God does not act according to debt, but according to mercy and goodness; for it has come to be that he grants life to favorable matter rather by mercy than by any other way.

Furthermore, what follows declares more clearly the things concerning providence and its care: 'your oversight has preserved my spirit,' saying 'spirit' for the soul. For although 'spirit' signifies many things, here it signifies the soul; for if James says, 'just as the body without the spirit is dead' (James 2:26), and Stephen, encountering God and saying, 'Lord, receive my spirit' (Acts 7:59), he signifies the soul. Having these [thoughts] within yourself, I know that you are able to do all things; nothing is unable for you.

God does not possess from without those things which he is said to possess; for everything that is, being simple and existing without mixture, does not take in anything from without; for he is uncomposite. For the Creator, and the Good, and the Light, and the All—if he is rightly theologized—is these things according to his essence. And 'you are able to do all things' should be heard faithfully and prudently, so that we do not fall into the folly of the opinionated.

And what is said is clear when used by a division thus: of the powers, some are active and others are passive. The active ones are such as we perform, and the passive ones are such as we undergo, which are directed toward the activities. Therefore, if it is said that God is able to do all things, one must not attribute to him also the passive powers; for it is not possible to say that he becomes something else—for he does not possess powers according to contingency—nor is it to be said that he is able to lie, or change, or deny himself. Therefore, I say, those things are possible for God which are fitting for God. For some, including Porphyry and his like, reason in a way that if all things are possible for God, including lying, and if all things are possible for the faithful, then he is able to make a bed and to make a man. But this is not what is meant, but just as, if it is said all things are possible for the physician...

Regarding medicine, I say that all things are possible to the pilot, those things which suit his art; so if I say all things are possible to God or to the faithful, I say this: that what suits God is possible for God, and what suits the faithful is possible for the faithful. These are the things made right through faith.

For the Scripture also knows this, it says concerning God: 'If we deny, he remains faithful. For he cannot deny himself' (2 Tim 2:13). And again: 'In whom it is impossible to lie to God' (Heb 6:18). Likewise, with understanding, the 'it is not able for you' must be avoided, which can be understood by analogy with what was said in the Gospel: 'All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made' (John 1:3). Consider, then, whether it is appropriate to think so in this way: evil is a 'non-being'; indeed, those participating in it are called non-existent because of their neglect: 'For you will not deliver the scepter to those who are not.' It is also said: 'Calling things that are not as though they were,' 'that he might bring to nothing the things that are'—so that this is saying: the non-existent and evil 'is not able' for you; for it is possible to turn away from sinning.

For if I sin, 'keep me; from lawlessness you have not made me innocent' (Ps 119:117). He says this reasonably; for since I know him to be creator and provider of himself and of all things, he follows by teaching also concerning his patience. For he himself knows, according to the blessed David, that 'he does not bring wrath every day' (Ps 103:9). But God guards the one sinning, not desiring him to sin—'for he does not desire the death of the sinner as [the desire for] repentance' (Ezek 33:11)—but so that, giving the law which forbids sinning, he might cause the one practicing it to hate evil. He also rebukes the friends who suppose that he suffers through sin, teaching them that God does not give [judgment] at the same time as the sinning, so that they too might reckon this according to themselves. And he teaches the turnability of human nature through 'from lawlessness you have not made me innocent,' while also presenting a pattern of moderation and indicating the succession of Adam, showing sin to be common to men. We do not say this, that the saints are subject to transgression by choice, but by succession, as was said. For just as a child born of an idolater does not have...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Nature of Job's Trials
english: Sin, which is like a stain, is caused by a corrupt upbringing; likewise, regarding the saints, one must consider a lapse as non-voluntary. Thus it has been said, 'For all have sinned' (Rom 3:23). We say that the sins of the saints are a path toward virtue.

Just as one learning to write, since he cannot write well immediately, stumbles during the learning process—not such that it is considered corrupt as if someone were writing evil by malicious intent—so also the one striving toward virtue, if he first stumbles through ignorance, is not to be punished. For if he were impious, woe to me! If he were righteous, I would not be able to bow my head. He might say, 'If I sin by choice, woe to me; but if, as we have previously stated, I have it only by succession from Adam, again I will not be able to bow my head as one completely cleansed of filth.' For of sins, those from our own choice stand as bad, but those [are different] as previously stated; for punishment follows those from choice, but purification is owed to those from ignorance. He might say, 'Even if I am righteous, I do not think greatly, knowing the obvious.' For many, having spoken highly of themselves, fell in practice.

And 'Pay attention, then, O Pharisee, speaking about God: did you not then speak truly?' (Luke 18:9); but the one who was self-important did not have the words accepted. It has been said regarding the lowly one, that 'this one descended having been justified by Him.' But I am full of dishonor. The sign of human weakness is thin, for man is full of dishonor by being a body surrounded by such a thing, about which Paul says: 'It is sown in dishonor, it is raised in glory' (1 Cor 15:43).

And I am hunted like a lion for slaughter. Thinking myself to be full of dishonor according to the previously stated sense, the enemy seeks to cast me down through those standing around, as if surrounding with dogs, and tries to envelop me with nets. But the lion is a great animal. It has been said: 'A lion is stronger than cattle.' 'For the righteous has become like a lion.' However, the one set out for a combatant knows that some beast is trying to hunt him; and this is the adversary, the devil. And he now calls the slip into sin a 'slaughter'; for slaughter is often said even regarding punishment. The magnitude of the assault against himself appears to exceed...

Through the saying, 'I am prowling like a lion' (Job 10:24), it is meant that the enemy is like a lion driving the wild beasts and not leaving him to avoid temptation. This is not arrogance, but it reveals the plot. For again, 'you turn me terribly' (Job 7:19). It shows that even if I prowl like a lion, so many things have surrounded me, but they do not attack by themselves; for the permission is small. If God had not permitted, the prowler would not have had the power.

The 'turning' must be understood actively as the change that happened to Job from wealth to poverty and from health to sickness; much of [text missing] has come to him. 'Renewing against me my distress' signifies the successive onslaughts of the attackers. For just as an enemy, being repelled from the opposing sides, prepares himself again to fight, the one who has taken authority devises new pains like against a man, increasing the affliction in magnitude.

This is shown by: 'while he was still speaking, another messenger came' (Job 33:23). For the calamities were frequent and successive. 'And with great wrath I used you; you brought trials upon me' (Job 7:18). And here again the magnitude of the afflictions is shown, not ceasing, but making it known to friends that this exceeding wrath is not, as one might think, because of sin, if one were to judge his life.

Anger here should not be understood as a passion, but as the attacking onslaught, just as Moses says to God: 'You sent out your wrath and consumed them like a reed' (Psalm 106:10). Some [suffer] because of sin; but here it is shown through 'you brought trials upon me' that it is not because of sins; for those being punished in this manner are not said to undergo trials. Thus, the bringing of trials must be understood not as if they had fallen upon them [by their own fault].

And this happens, which the disciples were taught in the prayer not to let happen: 'lead us not into temptation' (Matthew 6:13). Why then did you bring me out of the womb, and I did not die? And my eye did not see, and as if I did not exist, I became. Someone might think this to be out of malice, but he is turned from what was said toward God: 'But it is otherwise with you...'
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.
